sections.title: The lost-update problem, step by step

blocks.caption: Two transactions decrement the same stock count

head: Fix
SQL
Notes
rows: UPDATE items SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = 7 AND stock > 0
Best when the logic fits in one statement
Second transaction waits; hold the lock briefly
UPDATE … SET stock = 4, version = 8 WHERE id = 7 AND version = 7
DB detects the conflict and aborts one

blocks.text: Multi-version concurrency control keeps old versions of rows. Each transaction reads from a snapshot as of its start (or each statement's start), so **readers never block writers and writers never block readers**. Writers to the same row still conflict. Old versions are cleaned up later (VACUUM in Postgres). This is why long-running transactions are harmful — they pin old versions and bloat tables.

cols.title: Pessimistic (locks)
pros: No wasted work under heavy contention
cons: Never hold locks across user think time

cols.title: Optimistic (version check / CAS)
pros: No locks held; great when conflicts are rare

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: For a web flow where the user edits a form for minutes, use optimistic concurrency with a version number (or HTTP ETag + If-Match). For a hot counter updated by many workers, use an atomic UPDATE or a pessimistic lock.

items: Transaction A locks row 1 then wants row 2; B locks row 2 then wants row 1 — both wait forever.
Databases detect cycles and abort one transaction; the application must retry.
Prevent by always acquiring locks in a consistent order (e.g. by id) and keeping transactions short.

cols.title: Two-phase commit (2PC)
cons: Blocking if the coordinator fails mid-protocol; slow; locks held across the network

cols.title: Sagas
pros: Each step commits locally; compensations undo
cons: No isolation between steps; compensations must be designed

items: Distributed locks (Redis SET NX PX, ZooKeeper/etcd leases) coordinate work across machines, but **leases can expire while the holder is paused**. Protect the resource with **fencing tokens**: each lock grant gets a monotonically increasing number and the storage rejects writes carrying an older token.

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: I'd avoid distributed transactions: do the critical write as one local transaction with a conditional update, publish an event via the outbox, and let downstream steps run as a saga with compensations.
